**The connection:**

**Mészáros és Mészáros Ipari, Kereskedelmi és Szolgáltató Kft.** (gmr_id: 536e994b-63d4-5354-a4de-1bcd38457653) holds **two contracts for railway track modernization**, both awarded by **NIF Zrt.** (Nemzeti Infrastruktúra Fejlesztő Zrt. — the National Infrastructure Development Company):

2. Modernization of the **Százhalombatta – Ercsi junction** railway line section (CPV 45234100 — railway construction works)

**What Fontem is**

Fontem is a European public-data platform. It brings together public records that are usually scattered across many national and EU sources, so a reader can search them in one place and follow the links between them. The holdings include:

- **EU public procurement** — contracts, awarding authorities, winning companies, CPV codes, integrity red flags

- **NUTS regions, taxonomy codes, legal acts** — the geographic and classification scaffolding that ties the above together

The platform is built around a knowledge graph, so the natural way to use it is to follow relationships: a contract → its buyer → its winner → the winner's parent company → its sanctions status, and so on.

args.content:
What the data actually shows

The draft's premise — that EU bodies spent heavily with Russian suppliers before sanctions — is not what the procurement record shows. Across the entire TED-derived contract graph, only 5 contracts are awarded to companies registered in Russia, with a combined value of €55,480,942.93. That is the whole universe, not a slice of it.

The 2020 cluster: three contracts, €55.06 million

Three contracts were published in 2020, all to a single supplier — OJSC "Power Machines", a Russian turbine manufacturer — and all awarded by AS "Latvenergo", the Latvian state-owned power utility, for the reconstruction of hydroelectric generators at the Ķeguma and Pļaviņu plants:

  • Contract 040138-2014, published 2020-01-02, value €30,862,249.55 — Ķeguma HES-2 generator reconstruction
  • Contract 390680-2013, published 2020-01-03, value €24,141,817.03 — Pļaviņu HES generators 1 and 3 reconstruction
  • Contract 011221-2019, published 2020-11-16, value €57,991.19 — plasma heating system for the COMPASS tokamak, awarded by the Czech Academy of Sciences' Institute of Plasma Physics to LLC "BINP-Plasma"

The TED notice IDs on the two Latvian contracts (-2014, -2013) indicate the original tenders date to 2013–2014; the 2020 publication reflects later award notices on contracts negotiated well before the 2022 invasion. These are not new spending — they are the tail of pre-existing procurement.

2021 to 2025: nothing

No contracts awarded to Russian-registered suppliers appear in the graph for 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 or 2025. The five-year gap is the most striking feature of the data.

2026: two contracts, €418,885.16

Two contracts surface in 2026, both awarded by Bulgarian buyers:

  • Contract 45406ac6-e6b2-4057-b888-4688ca7157a4, published 2026-01-06, value €342,610.00 — spare parts for reactor coolant pumps (ГЦН-195М), awarded by Kozloduy NPP (Bulgaria's nuclear plant) to Rosatom Service AD
  • Contract 4e8ea029-ae6c-4c28-b38a-daa7052f14f6, published 2026-01-30, value €76,275.16 — one-year building security contract for the Centre of the Republic of Bulgaria's Industry in Moscow, awarded to a representative of a Russian private security firm

The 2026 total is 0.76% of the 2020 total. The pattern is consistent with sanctions enforcement: the large pre-2022 infrastructure deals are gone, and what remains is narrow — nuclear spare parts tied to long-running dependencies, and a Bulgarian government office physically located in Moscow.

What the data does not show

  • No EU institutions. All five buyers are national bodies in Latvia, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria. EU institutional procurement is not represented here.
  • No sanctioned suppliers. None of the five Russian winners (Power Machines, BINP-Plasma, Rosatom Service, the Moscow security firm) appear in the EU sanctions graph. Two other Russian companies in the database — Rosbank and Surgutneftegaz — are sanctioned, but neither holds EU contracts.
  • Russian presence in the database is not the same as Russian presence in EU spending. The graph contains 1,861 companies registered in Russia; only 5 of them (0.27%) hold EU procurement contracts.

Bottom line

The honest reading of the data is the opposite of the draft's framing. EU public procurement did not "spend heavily" with Russian suppliers before sanctions — it spent €55 million across three contracts, almost all of it on a single Latvian hydro refurbishment programme. After 2022, that drops to €418,885 across two contracts, both in Bulgaria, both tied to legacy dependencies. The story is not collapse from a high base; it is the near-disappearance of a small flow.
